A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same noise-preference study and retain identifiable methods, experiments, and analyses. Their complete text, figures, equations, and Appendices A-C are readable and support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original trained-network experiments on function computation, maze navigation, and single-neuron regulation, together with numerical fixed-point analyses.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds cognitive-task, path-integration, feedforward-network, activation-function, and training-run experiments.

M1.justification: The central CTRNN update rules, noise-in/noise-out formulations, and fixed-point procedure are retained. v2 adds a feedforward adaptation with two 100-unit hidden layers and extends the single-neuron regulator from ReLU to tanh (Appendices A and B.5), introducing model variants without redesigning the central approach.

E1.justification: v2 retains function computation, maze navigation, and regulation, while adding six cognitive tasks: ReactPro/ReactAnti, MemoryPro/MemoryAnti, and DelayPro/DelayAnti. It also adds two-dimensional path integration, extending coverage to stimulus-response rules, memory, delayed responses, and position estimation from movement cues (Sections 2.2.3-2.2.4).

E2.justification: The corresponding function-computation comparisons retain noise-in and noise-out networks and their noise-level controls. The added MLP and tanh experiments investigate architectural dependencies rather than introduce competing benchmark methods. Cited task implementations are not newly evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: v2 adds training-noise sweeps beyond the original function-computation setting (Figures 2b and A2), plus protocols for the new experiments. These include 15,000 cognitive-task training batches with doubled sampling of memory tasks, 100-step path-integration trials, and 20,000 MLP training batches (Appendices A-B). Settings for the retained experiments are largely unchanged.

E4.justification: New analyses test dependence on training-noise magnitude, rectification through ReLU versus tanh, recurrence through feedforward MLPs, and initialization through repeated training runs (Figures 2b, 3e, 6b, A1-A2). These substantially extend the original fixed-point prediction and ReLU regulator analyses.

E5.justification: Figure A1 newly reports four independent training runs with different initializations and noise seeds, displaying their individual error curves. v1 already reported error standard deviations and 300-sample Monte Carlo estimation, but lacked this across-training-run evidence. No confidence intervals or significance tests are introduced.

E6.justification: v2 adds cognitive-task, path-integration, MLP, tanh-regulator, training-noise, and replication results. New findings include zero-noise preference at sufficiently low training noise and sharper preference but worse optimal error as training noise increases (Figure 2b). The original principal curves are retained; these are additional results under expanded conditions, not same-setting performance improvements.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects its first branch condition from x >= 0 to x <= 0, repairing the overlapping conditions in the piecewise Ornstein-Uhlenbeck example. The principal fixed-point reasoning and Appendix C objectives remain unchanged; no substantial new proof framework is added.

C1.justification: The abstract expands the contribution beyond the original CTRNN demonstrations to diverse cognitive tasks, path integration, and feedforward networks. It also qualifies preference for the training noise as approximate and dependent on sufficiently large training noise, refining the original emphasis on matching the training level.

C2.justification: Sections 3.5 and 4 substantially expand the saturation-versus-coupling explanation and distinguish training stabilization from generalization benefits. v2 discusses applicability beyond rectifying, fixed-point networks and updates the remaining limitations to include unexplored limit-cycle dynamics and the unquantified relative regularization effectiveness of noise-in versus noise-out.

D1.justification: Appendices A-B add MLP architecture, regularization and optimizer settings, cognitive-task sampling and encoding choices, and path-generation distributions, boundary handling, and trial lengths. Appendix A also newly states that experimental code is supplied as Supplementary Material, although its availability cannot be verified from the PDFs alone.

R1.justification: v2 adds literature on path integration and noise-dependent biological computation. Noise-out models are now grounded in prior neuroscience work rather than introduced solely for didactic purposes, and Koren et al. (2025) motivates an energy-efficiency qualification. The central positioning relative to stochastic resonance remains.

P1.justification: v2 reworks the abstract, several Results passages, and Future work, substantially expanding the mechanistic explanation. The Discussion is reorganized from two subsections into four covering regularization, broader relevance, stochastic resonance, and future work. The overall Methods/Results and Appendix A-C framework is retained.

P2.justification: Figure 2 gains a training-noise panel, Figure 3 expands from two to five panels, and Figure 6 gains a full tanh comparison. New appendix Figures A1-A2 display replication and noise-out sweeps. Figures 4-5 are rearranged, and Figure 4's noise-axis label is corrected from variance to standard deviation.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially addresses v1's limited evidence for generality and repeatability through path-integration, cognitive-task, feedforward, tanh, training-noise, and repeated-run tests. These additions establish meaningful applicability boundaries and qualify the training-noise-matching claim. Expanded implementation details and discussion improve assessability. The gains outweigh localized reporting problems, including Section 4.1's reversed noise-in/noise-out label and Appendix B.5's nonnegative setpoint range despite negative tanh setpoints in Figure 6b.
